newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY SAYS RUSSIA HAS OBSOLETE VIEW OF NATO.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY SAYS RUSSIA HAS OBSOLETE VIEW OF NATO.

text.p: Hungary said Russia's opposition to the enlargement of NATO was based on an obsolete view and dismissed as "nonsense" the idea that enlargement to include the central European states posed a threat to Moscow.
"One of the problems is that the Russian leadership still maintains a rather obsolete view of NATO as they consider it," Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

Hungary is considered certain to be among the first group of countries, along with Czech republic and Poland, to be invited to join an enlarged North Atlantic Treaty Organisation at the alliance's next summit to be held in Madrid in June.
"I am absolutely certain (the idea) that the accession of those that are widely considered the most advanced to join ..would turn over the military balance in the region is nonsense," Kovacs said.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said at the World Economic Forum at Davos at the weekend that NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana was "wrong" in saying there was no threat to Russia implicit in NATO accepting new members.
Chernomyrdin contended that NATO had not changed its basic nature since Cold War days but Kovacs said it was Moscow which was stuck in the past.

"(The Russians) claim to consider NATO as a purely military organisation but if I see the role NATO has been playing in former Yugoslavia it was an absolutely positive role because it established peace," he said.
"No other institution such as the United Nations or the OSCE could establish peace in Bosnia."

NATO was charged with implementing the Dayton peace agreement signed in December 1995 which ended the three-year war in Bosnia after a perceived failure by the United Nations and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to enforce earlier ceasefires.

Kovacs said NATO, both by ruling out early membership for the Baltic States and by stating it had no intention of stationing nuclear weapons in Central Europe, had taken away the biggest reasons for Russia to feel threatened.
"The Russians apparently wanted to increase their bargaining position...on the geographical scope of the enlargement, and the NATO answer is 'No Balts'," he said.

"They (also want) not to have the military infrastructure getting to Russian territory and the NATO answer was the declaration by its foreign ministers that it doesn't want to deploy nuclear weapons on the territories of the new members."
Kovacs added that current efforts to come to an agreement on Russia's relationship with NATO removes the final threat to Moscow.
"They don't really feel the enlargement as a genuine direct security threat," he said. "(But) if Russia wants to oppose enlargement because of political prestige that's another issue."
